title: Portugal Digital Nomad Visa 2026: D8 Guide
metaDescription: Portugal digital nomad visa 2026: D8 needs 3,680 euros a month remote income, 11,040 euros savings, NIF and housing proof. Two routes explained.
headline: Portugal Digital Nomad Visa (D8) 2026: Income, Routes & Process

sections.title: What the D8 visa is and who qualifies
sections.content:
Portugal's D8 digital nomad visa, introduced in October 2022, lets non-EU, non-EEA and non-Swiss remote workers live in Portugal while working for employers or clients outside Portugal. It is an active-income route: pensions, rents or dividends alone belong on the D7 passive-income visa, and consulates increasingly push remote workers onto the D8.

You must work remotely for a foreign employer, freelance clients abroad, or your own company outside Portugal, and you cannot work for Portuguese companies on the D8. The income must be earned remotely and evidenced over the last three months, not merely promised in a future contract.

sections.title: Income and savings thresholds for 2026
sections.content:
For 2026 the monthly remote income threshold is 3,680 euros, set at four times Portugal's minimum wage of 920 euros, averaged over the last three months. The savings figure most guides cite is 11,040 euros, or twelve times the minimum wage, for the main applicant, though some consulates ask for less, so check your consulate's checklist.

Family members raise the bar: add 50% of the minimum wage, 460 euros a month, for a spouse or second adult, and 30%, 276 euros, for each child, with matching savings additions. A couple therefore needs about 4,140 euros a month, and a couple with one child about 4,416 euros a month.

sections.title: Two routes: temporary stay versus residence
sections.content:
The D8 comes in two forms. The temporary stay visa lasts up to one year and suits a trial relocation, but it does not lead to a residence permit or count toward long-term status. The residence visa is valid four months for entry, during which you attend AIMA, the immigration agency, to obtain a two-year residence permit renewable for three more years.

The residence route is the path to permanent residence and eventual citizenship, which generally requires ten years of residence for most nationalities, seven for EU and Portuguese-speaking-country nationals, plus A2 Portuguese. Consulates have 60 days by law to decide a residence visa, and AIMA then has 90 to 120 days for the permit.

sections.title: Documents, taxes and practical setup
sections.content:
The standard file includes an employment contract or freelance agreements with recurring invoices, three months of payslips or invoices with matching bank statements, a tax residence document, a Portuguese NIF tax number and bank account, a lease or property deed, a clean criminal record, and health insurance. Fees run to a few hundred euros per person across consular and card charges.

Residence-route holders must actually live in Portugal, within absence limits similar to the D7, and tax residence follows. The old non-habitual resident regime is closed to new applicants, though a narrower 20% flat-rate regime exists for listed high-value activities, so take tax advice before assuming a rate.

faqs.q: What is the minimum income for Portugal's digital nomad visa in 2026?
faqs.a: The 2026 threshold is 3,680 euros a month in remote income, calculated as four times Portugal's minimum wage of 920 euros and averaged over the last three months. Add 460 euros a month for a spouse or second adult and 276 euros for each child, and expect a savings balance near 11,040 euros for the main applicant.

faqs.q: What is the difference between the D7 and D8 visas?
faqs.a: The D7 is for passive income such as pensions, rents, dividends or interest, from 920 euros a month in 2026, while the D8 is for active remote work at 3,680 euros a month. Remote workers who apply on the D7 risk refusal or redirection, because consulates now steer people with employment or freelance income onto the D8 route.

faqs.q: Should I choose the temporary stay or residence D8 route?
faqs.a: Choose the temporary stay visa, valid one year, for a short trial that does not lead to residence status. Choose the residence visa if you want to settle: it gives four months to enter and apply at AIMA for a two-year residence permit, renewable for three years, counting toward permanent residence and eventual citizenship.

faqs.q: Can I bring my family on the D8 visa?
faqs.a: Yes, a spouse or partner, children and dependent parents can apply, but you must show extra means for each: 460 euros a month for an additional adult and 276 euros for each child, with matching savings. Family reunification after arrival is subject to a two-year sponsor rule, except for minor children and a spouse who is their other parent.

faqs.q: Can I work for a Portuguese company on the D8?
faqs.a: No, D8 income must come from outside Portugal, and you cannot work for Portuguese companies or serve clients based in Portugal. You may open a Portuguese company to manage international income if structured carefully, but the underlying clients and income must remain foreign for the visa to stay valid.
